title: Vaisakhi: the procession
hookLine: the Granth is carried through the streets, led by five Sikhs in saffron

cards: It's a spring morning in a city far from Punjab. A main road has been closed. People are sweeping it, and some are washing it down, though it's already clean.
Then you hear it coming: drums, and singing, a whole street of voices. Five figures walk at the front in saffron robes and turbans, swords held upright.
Behind them rolls a float covered in flowers, and on it, under a canopy, someone waving a whisk over a book. Behind that, a river of people, singing. The kirtan has left the building.

teach.b: It's called a nagar kirtan. Nagar means town; kirtan, you know, is singing the Guru's hymns. So: kirtan through the town.
Many are held around Vaisakhi, and others on gurpurabs, the Gurus' anniversaries, through the year. Everything you learned at the gurdwara is here, just outdoors.
The Guru Granth Sahib rides in a palki on a decorated float, under a canopy, with someone in attendance waving the chaur.

teach.h: FIVE IN FRONT, THE GRANTH BEHIND.
teach.b: At the front walk five Sikhs representing the Panj Pyare, the beloved five of 1699, in saffron or blue, often barefoot, carrying swords. Often the Nishan Sahib is carried too.

Ahead of them all, volunteers sweep and wash the road, as you'd prepare a path for royalty. Behind comes the sangat, singing. Along the way you'll often see gatka, the Sikh martial art, performed with sticks and swords.

teach.h: THE ROAD SWEPT, THE FOOD FREE.
teach.b: And all along the route, families set up stalls handing out free food and drinks to anyone passing: samosas, pakoras, sweets, water, tea. It's langar, moved onto the sidewalk.

In cities in Canada, the United States and Britain, a nagar kirtan can fill whole streets, and plenty of the people eating along the route aren't Sikh at all. Why take the Guru into the street? Partly celebration.
Partly to share: the gurdwara's doors are always open, but here the gurdwara walks out to meet people.
And partly as a reminder that the Guru's word isn't meant to stay indoors. It's meant for the whole town.

how: At Vaisakhi and on gurpurabs, Sikhs hold nagar kirtans: the Guru Granth Sahib is carried through the streets on a decorated float, led by five Sikhs representing the Panj Pyare, with the sangat singing and free food offered along the route.

o: the Guru's hymns sung in procession through the town
the free food stalls set up along a festival route
a concert of hymns held inside the gurdwara hall

games.q: what's in the procession — tap the pairs.

s: the road ahead of a nagar kirtan is swept and washed
as you'd prepare a path for royalty.
the free food along the route is only for Sikhs
it's langar on the sidewalk, for anyone passing.
nagar kirtans happen only at Vaisakhi
many are at Vaisakhi, and others on gurpurabs through the year.

games.q: you're watching a nagar kirtan and someone at a roadside stall hands you a samosa. you're not Sikh. what do you do?
o: take it and say thank you.
games.why: it's langar on the sidewalk, given to anyone. taking it with thanks is exactly the point.

practice: If you can, find a nagar kirtan video and watch a minute of it: the five at the front, the float, the singing crowd.
Or, if you'd rather stay quiet, close your eyes and picture a street you know well swept clean, a song coming down it, and food handed out free on every corner. Who would you want to feed?

wordCard.voice: Nagar kirtan. Singing through the town: the Guru Granth Sahib carried in procession, led by five Sikhs in saffron, with food for everyone along the way.

carryVoice: Your line: the song walks outside. Drums first, then the five, then everyone. Day one hundred forty-six, done.
